 Some Social Security Checks Arrived a Day Early Today. December’s Has to Last 35 Days
 By Danielle Liverance 
 Published November 10, 2026, 6:45am ET · 6 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Benefits due Wednesday, Nov. 11 (birthdays on the 1st through the 10th) are paid today, Tuesday, Nov. 10, because Veterans Day is a federal holiday; Nov. 18 and Nov. 25 payments do not move, and SSI is unaffected (paid Oct. 30 for November, Dec. 1 for December).
 The early deposit has to cover 29 days instead of 28, and the Dec. 9 check has to last 35 days, to Jan. 13. For a widow on $2,100 a month ($1,897 after the $202.90 Part B premium), that is $54.20 a day in December against $67.75 in a normal month.
 The 3.6% COLA starts with the January payment ($2,175.60 before Medicare for her); the 2027 Part B premium is still unannounced, with $209.50 projected. Stocks trade Wednesday; banks, the bond market and the post office are closed.

 Social Security is paying its second-Wednesday checks today, Tuesday, Nov. 10, a day early, because Wednesday, Nov. 11, is Veterans Day. The payment covers everyone whose benefit lands on the second Wednesday: retirees, survivors and disabled workers whose birthday, or whose spouse’s birthday, falls on the 1st through the 10th of the month.
 The rule is Social Security’s own. "If your regularly scheduled payment date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal public holiday, benefits will be paid the business day before your due date," the agency says in its payment FAQ. Veterans Day is a legal public holiday, so the deposit moves to Tuesday. The Federal Reserve, which clears the deposits, is closed Wednesday along with the banks.
 An early deposit is the same money arriving sooner, and that is the part to plan around. If you are in this group, the dollars that landed today have to cover 29 days instead of the usual 28, because your next check comes on its normal date, Wednesday, Dec. 9. Your December check then has to stretch 35 days, to the first January payment on Wednesday, Jan. 13. For anyone with a bill due this week, the extra day is a help. For anyone who spends to the deposit, it is a day of float that has to be paid back in December.
 Who gets paid today, and who waits
 Social Security pays in four groups. If you started benefits before May 1997, or you get both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, you were paid on Nov. 3, a Tuesday, on schedule. The second-Wednesday group is paid today. If your birthday is on the 11th through the 20th, you are paid on the third Wednesday, Nov. 18, and if it is on the 21st through the 31st, on the fourth Wednesday, Nov. 25. Nov. 25 is the day before Thanksgiving and an ordinary business day, so that payment does not move.
 Supplemental Security Income is not affected this week. SSI pays on the 1st of the month. November’s SSI payment went out on Friday, Oct. 30, because Nov. 1 was a Sunday, and December’s lands on Tuesday, Dec. 1, on schedule.
 The birthday that sets your day belongs to the worker whose record the benefit comes from. If you draw a survivor benefit, you are paid on your late husband’s or wife’s birthday schedule, and a spousal benefit follows the worker’s birthday, according to Social Security’s 2026 guide for retirement and survivor beneficiaries. If the deposit is not in your account today, Social Security’s advice is to call your bank first, since banks post federal deposits at different hours, and then the agency at 1-800-772-1213. For the few people still paid by paper check, the mail does not run Wednesday: the Postal Service is closed for the holiday.
 What else closes Wednesday
 Federal offices, the Federal Reserve and most banks are closed on Veterans Day. The stock market is open: the New York Stock Exchange does not list Nov. 11 among its 2026 holidays, so stocks trade normally. The bond market is closed, on the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association’s recommendation, so Treasury yields, and the mortgage rates that follow them, do not update until Thursday.
 One widow’s check: the same $1,897, one more day
 Take Joan, 74, widowed three years ago in Ohio, and in the second-Wednesday group because her late husband was born on the 6th. Her survivor benefit is $2,100 a month before Medicare. The standard Part B premium of $202.90 comes out first, leaving $1,897.10, and Social Security rounds the deposit down to the whole dollar, so $1,897 landed this morning.
 She runs the month on that deposit and leaves the $180,000 IRA she inherited from her husband alone, except for the withdrawal the IRS requires. Her budget looks like this:
 Property tax, insurance and upkeep on a paid-off house: $560
 Medigap and Part D premiums: $230
 Groceries: $450
 Electric, gas and water: $210
 Car insurance and gas: $210
 Phone and internet: $95
 That is $1,755 of bills against a $1,897 deposit, which leaves $142 a cycle for everything else, about $5 a day over the usual 28 days. The amounts are an example, and yours will differ, but the shape is common: most of your check is spoken for before it arrives.
 Today’s early deposit changes the arithmetic by one day. Spread over 29 days instead of 28, $1,897 is $65.41 a day instead of $67.75, a difference of $2.34 a day. The cushion falls from $5.07 a day to $4.90. If her autopays are set for the 11th, nothing changes except that the money is already there.
 December is the stretch to plan for. The check you get on Dec. 9 has to last until Jan. 13, 35 days, through Christmas, a heating bill and whatever renews in early January. At $1,897 that is $54.20 a day, and the $142 cushion shrinks to about $4 a day. The same five-week gap arrives for the third-Wednesday group, from Dec. 16 to Jan. 20, and the fourth, from Dec. 23 to Jan. 27.
 The fix for Joan is already sitting in her IRA. At 74 the IRS requires her to withdraw at least $7,059 from the $180,000 balance by Dec. 31, under the Uniform Lifetime Table’s divisor of 25.5. One extra week of her budget at the November rate is about $474. Taking the required withdrawal in early December, and parking one week of it in checking, covers the long gap without selling anything she did not already have to sell. The withdrawal is taxable income whenever she takes it, so a December date costs her nothing extra.
 January: the raise, and the number still missing
 Your first check with the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment comes in January: Jan. 13 if you are in Joan’s group. Social Security announced a 3.6% increase on Oct. 14, covering 76 million people on Social Security and SSI. Her $2,100 becomes $2,175.60, a raise of $75.60 a month before Medicare, in line with the average retired worker, whose benefit goes from $2,095 to $2,170.
 What comes out of it is still unknown. Medicare has not announced the 2027 Part B premium; last year’s figure came on Nov. 14. The Medicare trustees’ June report projected $209.50, up $6.60. At that premium, Joan’s January deposit would be $1,966, or $69 more than today’s. If the premium stayed at $202.90, the deposit would be $1,972. Social Security mails the notice with your exact amount in December, and if you sign up for digital notices in a my Social Security account by Nov. 18 you can read it online up to three weeks earlier.
 Two groups get their January money in December. SSI’s Jan. 1 payment and the Jan. 3 Social Security payment both arrive on Thursday, Dec. 31, because Jan. 1 is a holiday and Jan. 3 is a Sunday. Those are the first payments at the new rate.
 The bottom line
 If you are paid on the second Wednesday, today’s deposit is Wednesday’s money arriving a day early, and no more. Set it against the bills through Dec. 8. The December check has to cover five weeks, to Jan. 13, and that is the gap to plan for now: a one-week cushion of about $474 on Joan’s budget, which a required IRA withdrawal taken in early December can fund. The January check brings the 3.6% raise, and the Part B premium that will come out of it should be known within days.
